Title: Diagnosis

Details: The bug report states that in WordUtils.abbreviate, when the `lower` parameter is greater than the length of the input string `str`, this causes a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException at the call to `str.substring(0, upper)`.

Inspecting the method WordUtils.abbreviate(String str, int lower, int upper, String appendToEnd) reveals the following:

1. If `upper` is -1 or greater than the length of the string, it is adjusted down to str.length().
2. If `upper` is less than `lower`, then `upper` is raised to `lower`.
3. But `lower` is never adjusted to be capped by str.length().
4. Afterwards, the code calls str.substring(0, upper), but if `lower > str.length()`, then the adjustment at line 623 sets upper=lower, which is greater than str.length(), triggering substring with an out-of-bounds index.
5. The failing test case calls abbreviate with `lower=15, upper=20` on a string "0123456789" whose length is 10.
6. During execution, `upper` is set to str.length() = 10 at line 619, but then because upper < lower (10 < 15) at line 622, upper is set to 15 (the value of lower).
7. However, `lower` was not adjusted down to str.length() and remains 15.
8. When substring(0, upper) is called on the string with length 10, upper=15, leading to StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

The root cause is failing to limit the `lower` parameter by the length of the input string before adjusting `upper`. The bug report's suggested fix to also adjust `lower` to be at most the length of the string before comparison and substring calls is correct. This prevents upper from being set outside the bounds of the string, avoiding the out-of-bounds exception.

Hence, this bug arises from the lack of capping the `lower` parameter to str.length(), causing illegal substring calls when lower is greater than str length, as demonstrated by the failing test case.

Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
